transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-04
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Sam Torres (Redwood CSM); Maya Patel (NovaHealth - Head of Data), Carlos Ruiz (NovaHealth - ML Eng), Leah Simmons (NovaHealth - Product), Dr. Omar H (clinical advisor)
Shared artifacts: sprint-3 results sheet (link: drive.redwood/nova/sprint3_results.csv), prompt set v3 (link: drive.redwood/nova/prompt_set_v3.md)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
- Quick review of sprint-3 quality metrics; identified regressions on rare PHI prompts (1.8% hallucination increase).
- SE proposed two prompt recalibrations + updated guardrail rules; agreed to run 1k regression and share results.
- Agreed next steps: regression run, SOW draft, PHI whitelist completion, infra deep-dive.

Topics: quality metrics, prompt variants, guardrails, scoring rubric, rollout canary strategy, latency impact of guardrails

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, quick roll call — Priya, Sam — you good?
[00:06] Priya: Yep hi all, ready.
[00:08] Maya: Hi, thanks. Umm we pushed the sprint updates and seen the sheet, gave it a look.
[00:15] Jordan: Great. Carlos, Leah — anything to call out before we jump in?
[00:18] Carlos: Just that we did a small manual review on 200 samples and noticed a couple fuzzy outputs on the PHI edge cases.
[00:24] Leah: And the product team is worried about user-facing hallucinations for those clinical notes.
[00:29] Priya: ok, so the sprint-3 report, top-line: overall QA scores held steady — precision around 0.93 for structured extraction — but we did see a bump in hallucination when prompts included obfuscated identifiers and nested temporals, so likely prompting failure rather than model drift.
[00:45] Maya: Can you — sorry — break down "hallucination" metric for us? I think our PMs interpret that differently.
[00:50] Priya: Sure. Our rubric flags answers with unsupported assertions or invented med dosages as hallucinations; the scoring is binary per example, then we report rate. For sprint-3 baseline we saw 2.6% and the flagged subset for PHI edge cases moved to 4.4% — so about +1.8 percent points.
[01:06] Jordan: Worth calling out we also changed the prompt template in v3 — the new system instruction tightened the persona but unfortunately made some idiosyncratic completions for nested ask.
[01:16] Carlos: Right, that matches what we saw. The new prompt does better on extraction but worse on ambiguous phrasing.
[01:22] Priya: So proposal — two parallel mitigations: (A) prompt recalibration (three variants: v3a conservative, v3b constrained-extraction, v3c context-window emphasis), and (B) rule-based guardrails that run post-generation to detect likely PHI hallucinations using a lightweight regex + medical-entity model.
[01:42] Leah: How much latency does the post-gen guardrail add? Our SLO is 600ms p95 for interactive flow.
[01:48] Priya: Good question. For the rule-only path it's negligible, but for ML-based entity check it's ~40-70ms extra at p95 on our dedicated infra. If you want zero impact, we can run the guardrail async and redact after — but UX tradeoff.
[02:02] Jordan: Also note that we can canary the guardrail on 10% traffic to measure false positives.
[02:08] Maya: That's sensible. I want to avoid redacting legitimate content too aggressively.
[02:11] Carlos: One more — when you say "dedicated infra" is that Redwood Dedicated? We're currently on hosted API pilot, right?
[02:17] Jordan: Yes hosted for pilot, but the dedicated numbers are just to give an idea of runtime overhead. The canary and rollout policies can be applied in-hosted too; it just impacts how quickly we can iterate.
[02:26] Priya: Back to scoring: we recommend using a composite score for the regression: 60% accuracy/precision on extraction, 25% hallucination penalty, 15% safety/TOX. We'll export the script we use to compute that so scoring is reproducible.
[02:40] Maya: Can the scoring script handle multi-turn context? Some of our prompts use conversation history.
[02:45] Priya: Yes — it strips history to the minimal prefix per your config; for evaluation we run both single-turn and full-context variants.
[02:52] Dr. Omar H: quick clinical note — some of the obfuscated ids mimic real lookups; if you're using simple regex we might need to add a couple of patterns.
[02:58] Priya: noted, we'll add those patterns as part of the guardrail.
[03:01] Jordan: I opened the sprint3_results.csv earlier; let's pull a couple examples. Priya, would you read sample 37?
[03:06] Priya: Sure — sample 37: prompt included "patient x with hx of CAD, med list shows Lipitor and lis" — expected: list of meds; model returned a plausible drug plus an invented dosage. Marked hallucination.
[03:20] Carlos: That's the one. We flagged that.
[03:22] Priya: Ok action: we'll add an instruction to not invent dosages and to respond with "unknown" if not certain — that's one heuristic in v3a.
[03:31] Leah: Will that reduce helpfulness in some cases? If the model says unknown too often, clinicians get frustrated.
[03:36] Priya: Right — hence v3b which focuses on constrained extraction only — force the model to output structured JSON with keys present/absent, and v3c which increases context window emphasis to disambiguate. We'll run all three and compare.
[03:49] Jordan: And we'll measure tradeoffs: extraction F1 vs hallucination rate and a simple utility score combining them.
[03:55] Maya: What's the plan for regression? Timing?
[03:58] Priya: We'll run the 1k-run across the three variants plus baseline — so 4k evals — should complete in ~48 hours on our test infra. Deliverable: CSV with per-prompt scores, aggregated metrics, and examples for manual review. Target share date 2025-06-09.
[04:14] Carlos: Also can you include the original prompt ID so we can trace in logging?
[04:18] Priya: Yes we'll include a mapping id and the request hash.
[04:22] Sam: Quick note on costs — running all four variants in parallel will bump the test cost; Jordan will include a rough cost estimate in SOW.
[04:29] Jordan: Yep will do.
[04:31] Maya: On compliance: we need to capture audit logs for any redaction or guardrail action for SOC2. Does Redwood produce that?
[04:38] Priya: Yes; we log guardrail triggers and the redaction event as part of the audit trail. Those logs can be shipped to your SIEM; we have S3 and Splunk integrations.
[04:46] Carlos: Do you support KMS key handling for any redacted content?
[04:50] Jordan: For the hosted pilot we offer envelope encryption and integration with customer-managed KMS for Private/Dedicated deployments; for this pilot we can add a pseudo-KMS flow for testing.
[04:59] Leah: We also had a question about model rollbacks — if one of the prompt variants causes regression, can we auto-fallback?
[05:05] Priya: Yes — Redwood has route-level fallback policies. You can map percentage traffic to fallback model or fallback behavior. We also support canary with automatic rollback if latency or error rate crosses threshold.
[05:15] Maya: Great. Could we get a runbook for that?
[05:18] Jordan: We'll attach the rollback/runbook to the SOW package.
[05:21] [06:00] (middle of call, screen share) Priya: I'm uploading the filter patterns now, see prompt_set_v3.md. There's a table showing the three variants and example tokens.
[06:30] Maya: Looking at examples — sample 412 is interesting: nested temporals — model inserted a future date that wasn't in context.
[06:38] Priya: That's likely due to system instruction ambiguity. We'll add an explicit "do not infer dates" constraint.
[06:44] Carlos: One more ask — can Redwood run the regression with the same random seed and beam settings as prod so it's apples-to-apples?
[06:50] Priya: We'll match the sampling parameters exactly for the baseline; the constrained variants may change decoding to beam=1 or temperature=0.0 for deterministic extraction. We'll note those differences.
[06:58] Jordan: On guardrails: team prefers a two-layer approach — fast regex for clear cases, then ML-based detector for fuzzy cases; we can tune thresholds to hit your desired FP/TP.
[07:09] Maya: What's the expected false-positive rate at current thresholds?
[07:12] Priya: For regex alone low FP but misses some; for ML-detector tuned to 0.85 threshold we saw TP 0.92, FP 0.12 on our validation slice. We can move threshold toward lower FP but lose some TP.
[07:25] Leah: Ok so we want a conservative FP < 0.10 if possible.
[07:29] Priya: We'll run threshold sweeps and include ROC curves in the report.
[07:34] Jordan: Any competitor concerns? Maya?
[07:36] Maya: We looked briefly at Anthropic's approach — they have stronger instruction-following on some long-form, but cost and latency were higher; we wanted Redwood for the better unit economics.
[07:47] Jordan: Good context.
[07:48] Priya: Any other technical blockers?
[07:50] Carlos: One: our logging currently scrubs a lot of PII before sharing. For the regression we can provide syntheticized logs; just need to map back.
[07:59] Jordan: That's fine — include mapping file.
[08:02] Maya: Quick question about evaluation rubric — can we add a "clinical harm" bucket? Something beyond hallucination that flags potentially dangerous misstatements?
[08:10] Priya: Yes, we already added a harm severity label on examples (none/minor/major) and will surface examples labeled major.
[08:17] Dr. Omar H: I'll help annotate a small sample for the severity labeling so thresholds are clinically meaningful.
[08:22] Priya: Appreciate that.
[08:24] Jordan: Ok wrap up time: Priya will run regression and share by 6/9; Jordan to send SOW by 6/11; customer to finalize whitelist by 6/8; infra deep-dive planned week of 6/16. Any other blockers?
[08:36] Maya: None from me.
[08:38] Carlos: All good.
[08:39] Leah: Thanks everyone.
[08:40] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with links and the runbook.
[08:43] (call ends)
notes: Transcript has occasional ASR errors (e.g., 'KV cach' might appear as 'KV cache' or 'KV cach'). References to external links are placeholders to shared drives.
